newsitem.title: CANADA: Financial markets nervous ahead of Canada election.
newsitem.headline: Financial markets nervous ahead of Canada election.

text.p: Canada's financial markets are nervous about the prospect of the right-wing Reform Party becoming the official opposition in Canada's June 2 election.

Reform is expected to win enough seats in its Western Canada stronghold to unseat the separatist Bloc Quebecois as the second biggest party in the next federal parliament. Prime Minister Jean Chretien's Liberal Party leads in the polls.

Stressing no special deals with Quebec and the equality of all 10 provinces, Reform leader Preston Manning put Quebec's future within Canada at the top of the campaign agenda. His approach has been been described by the other parties as divisive and even bigoted.
"Anything that puts the national unity issue front and center is a negative for financial markets. Both the Bloc and Reform do that," said John McCallum, chief economist with Royal Bank of Canada.

A Globe and Mail/Environics Research Group poll released on Friday showed the Liberals positioned to win 39 percent of the vote, the Conservatives 20 percent, Reform 19 percent, the New Democrats 11 percent and the Bloc 9 percent.
A computerized projection on a district-by-district basis gave Reform 55 seats in the 301-seat parliament -- enough to become the official opposition to the Liberals.
In the 1993 election, the Bloc Quebecois won 54 seats -- two more than Reform.
Although winning official opposition status was the top objective for Reform in the campaign, some pundits had predicted the party was in decline and would be eclipsed by the rival Conservatives.
For many economists, a Liberal majority coupled with a Conservative opposition would be a match made in heaven.

"Markets feel more comfortable with a Conservative opposition on the grounds that they represent a similar approach to Quebec," said Mario Angastiniotis, economist with research firm MMS International in Toronto.
The Conservatives, like the Liberals, favor recognizing French-speaking Quebec as a "distinct society" within Canada.
But the dream team parliament may have been derailed by the playing of the the national unity issue.

The return of Canada's constitutional demons -- the federal government failed twice in the past decade to have Quebec sign the Constitution -- unleashed a torrent of emotion in a country still haunted by the unity forces' razor-thin victory in the 1995 Quebec sovereignty referendum.
Quebeckers voted just 50.6 percent to 49.4 percent in the referendum to remain in Canada.
Reform's controversial Quebec strategy appeared to work in opinion polls, with the party's popularity gaining in Western Canada.
Financial markets got the jitters when a series of polls this week showed Liberal support slipping below the 40 percent threshold considered necessary for a majority government.
The Canadian dollar shed almost one U.S cent and Canadian bonds underperformed U.S. treasuries.
"A Liberal minority with a Reform opposition is the worst-case scenario for the Canadian dollar," Angastiniotis said.
